## Results

To elucidate the role of key molecular structures in regulating amorphous phase formation during melt-processable energetic compounds40–43. we conducted a systematic investigation of representative small-molecule explosives spanning three structural classes (imidazole derivatives, benzene derivatives, and polycyclic compounds) (Supplementary Fig. 1). To investigate the phase transition behavior, the melts were rapidly cooled at 50 K/min (Supplementary Fig. 2–4). The DSC cooling curves reveal crystallisation exothermic peaks (the crystallization temperature, T ) for 4-methoxy-1-methyl-3,5-dinitro-1 H -pyrazole (DMDNP), 1,3-dinitrobenzene (DNB), 2,4-dinitroanisole (DNAN) and benzotrifuroxan (BTF) during cooling (Supplementary Fig. 2c-d, 3d, 4b). This phenomenon indicates that even at high cooling rates, these compounds exhibit a strong tendency to form ordered crystalline structures. In stark contrast, the T of 3,4-dinitropyrazole (DNP), 1-methyl-3,4,5-trinitropyrazole (MTNP), 2,4,6-trinitro-3,5-difluorophenyl methyl ether (DFTNAN), and 3,4-dinitrofurazanfuroxan (DNT F) were not detected during cooling (Supplementary Fig. 2b, 3a-b, 4a), suggesting their melts may be supercooled and form metastable amorphous states (supercooled liquids or glassy states). Subsequent reheating confirmed that DNP, DFTNAN, and DNTF each exhibited distinct endothermic transitions corresponding to the glass transition temperature (T ), thereby verifying their glassy state. After subsequent heating, distinct crystallization exothermic peaks (T ) were observed at -7.82 °C, 26.53 °C, 27.30 °C, and 24.18 °C for DFTNAN, DNP, MTNP, and DNTF, respectively. This result clearly indicates that as the temperature rises to near ambient conditions, molecules acquire sufficient kinetic energy to drive the system from a disordered metastable state to ordered crystalline structure. Therefore, these amorphous phases lack the necessary structural stability within typical operating temperature ranges (e.g., room temperature to 50 °C), limiting their practical application prospects.

In order to investigate the decisive factors governing the formation and stability of amorphous structures at the molecular level, the molecular planarity parameter (MPP) and molecular surface deviation (SDP) were introduced to quantify the planar characteristics of molecules44. Smaller values indicate that the molecular structure is closer to a perfect planar configuration. The analysis indicates that molecules exhibiting strong crystallisation tendencies, such as DMDNP, DNB, DNAN, and BTF, possess a greater planarity. Conversely, the molecules DNP, MTNP, DFTNAN, and DNTF, which form amorphous states upon rapid cooling, show greater atomic deviation from the plane and poorer planarity. These results suggest that reduced molecular planarity (molecular planarity parameter, MPP > 0.3) is a key initial factor in suppressing crystallization and promoting amorphous phase formation (Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 1). This is because non-planar structures (such as the steric hindrance of methoxy groups in DNAN or the rotatable flexible furan ring in DNTF) effectively increase steric hindrance, thereby impeding the formation of ordered lattices. However, non-planarity alone is insufficient to achieve physically stable amorphous structures with practical utility. DNP exhibits high molecular rigidity, lacks flexible functional groups, possesses poor planarity (MPP = 0.367), and successfully forms an amorphous state. Notably, the glass transition temperature (T ) of the amorphous DNP (T = −19.67 °C) is higher than that of the DFTNAN, which exhibits poorer planarity (MPP = 0.519, T = −46.48 °C). We speculate that this may be due to the presence of both hydrogen bond donors and acceptors within DNP, which form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. This is crucial for inhibiting the ordered rearrangement of molecules and enhancing the stability of the amorphous state.

With the above understanding, the amorphous organic small molecules can be successfully synthesised from the synergy of multiple factors. This can be achieved by modulating the molecular backbone and functional groups to reduce molecular planarity, whilst simultaneously introducing hydrogen bond donors and acceptors to enhance intermolecular interactions. Under this design principle, DATNBI was selected as the model molecule for preparing structurally stable amorphous energetic materials. Its advantage lies in the conformational complexity imparted by its double imidazole skeleton, which further increases steric hindrance (Supplementary Fig. 6) and restricts the freedom of molecular motion. Moreover, DATNBI incorporates both diamino (strong hydrogen bond donors) and dinitro (strong hydrogen bond acceptors) groups within its molecular structure. This configuration provides multiple hydrogen bonding sites, facilitating the formation of a stronger, more stable intermolecular hydrogen bond network.

Amorphous DATNBI (AEM-DATNBI) was constructed through single-crystal thermal phase transition pathway, crystalline DATNBI (CEM-DATNBI) was melted at 263 °C and then rapidly quenched to freeze its disordered state (Figure 2a). AEM-DATNBI exhibited a significantly higher glass transition temperature (T = 59.67 °C) and a cold crystallization exotherm occurring at 98.26 °C (Figure 2b). This elevated T and cold-crystallization temperature indicate that DATNBI can maintain a stable amorphous state over a substantially wider temperature window compared to the other glass formers32. Polarized optical microscopy (POM) provided compelling visual evidence for the structural transformation. CEM-DATNBI showed birefringence-induced coloration (Supplementary Fig. 7a), contrasting sharply with the featureless dark field of its amorphous counterpart (Supplementary Fig. 7b), confirming isotropic structural homogeneity. At the microscale, CEM-DATNBI appeared as cubic structures with significant surface roughness and defects (Supplementary Fig. 8), whereas the amorphous solid presented as smooth, dense, and uniform irregular blocks (Figure 2a). Furthermore, X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns revealed the disappearance of characteristic diffraction signals from crystalline DATNBI in AEM-DATNBI, with broad peaks observed at 17.1° and 23.5° (Figure 2c), marking the dissolution of long-range order and the establishment of the amorphous state. The room temperature X-ray total scattering of AEM-DATNBPI was further performed to study its structural characteristic. Subsequent normalized, and Fourier transformed yielded the radial distribution function (RDF) (Supplementary Fig. 9a). RDF results demonstrate that distinct peaks at short-range distances (<5 Å) from molecular aggregation, while the weakening of peaks beyond 5 Å confirmed the absence of periodic packing. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations corroborated these observations (Supplementary Fig. 9b).

Critically, spectroscopic and chromatographic analyses confirmed unaltered molecular integrity. FTIR spectra (Figure 2d) showed identical functional group signatures between crystalline and amorphous states, though N-H stretching (3250 cm⁻¹) and bending modes (1500–1625 cm⁻¹) shifted due to hydrogen-bond reorganization and conformational polymorphism45,46. Consistency in HPLC retention times (Supplementary Fig. 10) and molecular weights (Supplementary Fig. 11) ruled out degradation. Calculated chemical purity exceeds 99.8% (external standard method) (Supplementary Fig. 12 and Supplementary Table 2). Furthermore, the chemical shifts of the imidazole ring in the 13C NMR spectra of AEM-DATNBI were found at 135.7, 134.3, and 131.6 ppm. The corresponding 1H NMR signal appeared at 6.98 ppm (Supplementary Fig. 13). These values are very similar to those of CEM-DATNBI47,48, further confirming that the amorphisation process has not disrupted its chemical structure.

Structural stability of AEM-DATNBI
Following confirmation of the amorphous structure and molecular integrity of AEM-DATNBI, its structural stability was further investigated. It starts to transform into a crystalline state when heated to 90 °C, as evidenced by XRD peaks matching those of α-DATNBI and γ-DATNBI (Figure 2e). The diffraction pattern at 100 °C revealed multiple sharp peaks, corresponding to the representative diffraction peaks of α-, β-, and γ-phases. It is easy to understand that the molecular mobility increases above the T prompting conformational rearrangement, driving the transition from amorphous to crystalline states. This process visually captured by POM (Supplementary Fig. 14), where isotropic amorphous regions transformed into birefringent crystalline domains. With heated induction crystallisation observed, we systematically evaluated the isothermal stability of amorphous AEM-DATNBI, focusing on its behavior near and above the glass transition temperature (T ). Close to the T (59.8 °C), AEM-DATNBI exhibited excellent structural stability over 24 hours at 60 °C. The stacked XRD patterns at 60°C (Figure 2f) consistently displayed a broad halo indicative of long-range disorder. As the isothermal test temperature increased to 100 °C (Supplementary Fig. 15), the physical stability of AEM-DATNBI progressively diminished, correlating with enhanced molecular mobility due to thermal activation above the T . Notably, during isothermal crystallization at 100 °C, AEM-DATNBI preferentially yielded γ-phase crystals (Supplementary Fig. 15d). This suggests that controlled isothermal crystallization of AEM-DATNBI can facilitate a rapid and straightforward conversion to γ-DATNBI.

To more realistically simulate temperature fluctuations in practical applications, the response of the material to dynamic thermal cycling was further investigated. The non-isothermal cycle (30 °C → 80 °C) revealed dynamic phase transition behavior (Figure 2g and Supplementary Fig. 16). The amorphous structure was maintained during heating, whereas subsequent cooling initiated the transformation of AEM-DATNBI towards a crystalline state (Figure 2g). This is attributed to the softening of AEM-DATNBI near its glass transition temperature (59.67 °C). The molecules undergo kinetically controlled rearrangement during cooling, transforming the local structure from short-range order to long-range order. Compared to prior work, such as the amorphization of PETN49, HNAB33, and TNT32, AEM-DATNBI exhibited relatively a better structural stability within the permissible temperature range (30-60 ℃). This structural stability is likely attributable to the fact that DATNBI possesses both amino and nitro groups form a three-dimensional hydrogen-bond network. This network impedes molecular rearrangement, thereby stabilising the amorphous phase, as corroborated by Supplementary Fig. 17. While AEM-DATNBI has achieved a degree of structural stability, further improvements are necessary to ensure that amorphous energetic materials remain stable under complex and variable application conditions.

Mechanism of AEM-DATNBI Formation
To further elucidate the formation mechanism of amorphous DATNBI, the real-time polarized optical microscopy (POM) captured its transition from crystalline to amorphous states. The β-DATNBI (crystalline state) first evolves into defective α-phase crystals (30-150 °C), followed by γ-phase restructuring (170-190 °C). The lattice structure is destroyed above 236°C, transitioning to a molten state. Finally, the molecule freezes to form an amorphous state upon quenching (Figure 3a). The structural evolution from crystalline to amorphous states is clearly documented in the in situ XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 18). During this process, the sharp β-phase diffraction peak successively undergoes α-phase and γ-phase transitions, ultimately disappearing entirely after melt quenching. This is replaced by broadened diffuse peaks at 17.1° and 23.5°, which confirm the destruction of the long-range ordered structure and amorphous formation. This process aligns with previous studies by our group on the polymorphic transitions of DATNBI50. At the crystalline level, the molecular packing pattern evolves from the wavy spatial arrangement of β-DATNBI to the cross-grid arrangement of γ-DATNBI, ultimately transforming into a completely disordered amorphous structure (Figure 3b). Infrared spectroscopy analysis revealed significant differences in the vibrational modes of -NH₂ groups among different polymorphs, particularly in the peak positions within the ranges of 3250 cm⁻¹ (N-H stretching vibration) and 1625–1500 cm⁻¹ (N-H bending vibration) (Figure 3c-d). The infrared absorption bands of AEM-DATNBI closely resemble those of γ-DATNBI, indicating that while it exhibits long-range disorder, it forms short-range cluster-like structures analogous to γ-DATNBI. This structural similarity facilitates amorphous phase formation. The infrared absorption frequencies of N-H (3361.3 cm⁻¹ and 929.5 cm⁻¹), N-C (1376.4 cm⁻¹), and -NO2 (1056.8 cm⁻¹) showed significant shifts compared to the crystalline state. The red-shifted N-O vibrational frequency indicates that the hydrogen bonding between N-H and O-N has been strengthened. Molecular dynamics simulations further confirmed an increase in the number of hydrogen bonds (Figure 3e), while the blue-shifted bending vibration frequency of N-H reflected the constraints imposed by random molecular arrangements on vibrations. In summary, the stable amorphous state achievable by DATNBI arises from the synergistic interplay between molecular architecture, intermolecular interactions, and phase transition kinetics. In terms of molecular engineering, the non-planar backbone disrupts crystalline packing, while dual functional groups (–NH₂/–NO₂) construct a robust hydrogen-bonding network. On the phase transition kinetics, thermally induced lattice disordering coupled with quenching captures the metastable state. In terms of conformational constraints, the distorted structure provides steric barrier effects, inhibiting molecular rearrangement and nucleation processes.

Self-healing capability and surface character of AEM-DATNBI
Interestingly, AEM-DATNBI exhibits temperature-activated self-repair capability, with surface cracks healing completely within 73 seconds at 60 °C, as directly observed by in situ optical microscopy at specific time intervals (Figure 4a). This phenomenon arises from hydrogen bond network reconfiguration enabled by softened molecular mobility. To further investigate the structural evolution of AEM-DATNBI during the self-healing process under in situ loading. The small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) to measure nanoscale pore defects in the solid (Supplementary Fig. 19 and 20). The SAXS results for AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI were converted into one-dimensional curves using Foxtort software, and the scattering data were corrected 51,52(Figure 4b-c). The scattering intensity of CEM-DATNBI was consistently higher than that of the amorphous phase. As the temperature gradually increased, the scattering intensity of the crystal remained almost unchanged, while that of AEM-DATNBI decreased by nearly an order of magnitude. Quantitative analysis of in situ SAXS data collected during heating from 30 °C to 110 °C revealed a total porosity reduction of 40.6% in the amorphous phase, while the crystalline phase showed a smaller decrease of 8.8%. Throughout this temperature range, the amorphous phase consistently exhibited lower porosity than the crystalline phase, as shown in Figure 4d. This distinctive microstructure effectively inhibits the formation of hot spots during impact and friction events, thus significantly mitigating the risk of accidental initiation. Thereby further unveiling its potential for practical applications.

Solid-solid surface contact phenomena are of critical importance in the processing and formulation development of explosives. We quantitatively evaluated binder compatibility through atomic-scale surface characterization, revealing fundamental differences between amorphous and crystalline systems. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) topographic analysis (Figure 4e) demonstrates that AEM-DATNBI achieves exceptional surface homogeneity with sub-nanometer roughness (R = 1.29 nm), contrasting sharply with layered growth patterns characteristic of CEM-DATNBI (R = 25.19 nm). This remarkable difference in surface morphology is attributed to the distinct structural arrangements of amorphous and crystalline phases. The enhanced interfacial adhesion of amorphous systems was quantified using F2314-functionalized AFM probes. Statistics and frequency counts are conducted to eliminate the random factors. Reliable tip-sample interaction force spectrum is obtained for CEM-DATNBI and AEM-DATNBI (Figure 4f and Supplementary Fig. 21). The adhesive force (F ) measured of CEM-DATNBI and AEM-DATNBI are 7.83 nN and 8.95 nN, respectively. This result showing 14.3% stronger binding forces compared to crystalline surface. These results provide important insights into interfacial interactions for explosive processing and formulation development. Contact angle measurements revealed the surface free energy of AEM-DATNBI was 38.3 mN/m, significantly lower than that of CEM-DATNBI (50.7 mN/m) (Figure 4g and Supplementary Fig. 22). The lower surface energy of AEM-DATNBI can be attributed to its disordered structure and high free volume53. The lack of long-range order in the amorphous phase allows surface molecules to rearrange and form lower energy configurations than in the crystalline phase, where rigid lattice structures restrict such restrict such motions.54. This structural flexibility contributes to the observed reduction in surface energy. The enhanced adhesion and lower surface energy of AEM-DATNBI suggest potential advantages in terms of enhancing structural stability and component adhesion capacity.

Energy Release and Mechanical sensitivity of AEM-DATNBI
As a specialized class of functional materials, the safety and energy release characteristics of explosives have long been a focal point of research. The thermal decomposition processes of AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI were evaluated using thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). As shown in Figure 5a, CEM-DATNBI displayed an endothermic melt at 236.1 °C followed by decomposition peaks at 263.2 °C and 271.8 °C50. the amorphous counterpart exhibited exothermic decomposition at reduced temperatures (247.2 °C and 263.0 °C), reflecting a 10 °C destabilization of the decomposition threshold, demonstrating the destabilizing influence of amorphization on thermal stability. This phenomenon is likely due to amorphous substable state features. Crucially, AEM-DATNBI achieved near-complete mass loss (97.4%) compared to crystalline samples (77.3%, Figure 5b). This 20.1% increase in mass loss indicates that the decomposition reaction of amorphous DATNBI is more complete. The gaseous products generated during the preparation process were analyzed to gain a deeper understanding of its thermal decomposition mechanism. The FT-IR and pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (PY-GCMS) spectra of their decomposition products are shown in Supplementary Fig. 23–24. It is observed from Supplementary Fig. 23 that the decomposition product types of AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI remain consistent, with primary gaseous products comprising N₂O, NO₂, NO, CO, CO₂, and H₂O. Supplementary Fig. 24 illustrates the relative concentration variations of several representative products. Compared to CEM-DATNBI, the gas products from AEM-DATNBI exhibit a significantly elevated relative concentration of N₂O/CO₂ (48% vs. 45%) and a marked increase in the relative concentration of NO (27% vs. 16%). Conversely, the relative content of CO decreased substantially (6% vs 26%). CO₂, and H₂O are products of highly oxidative processes, whereas CO signifies incomplete oxidation. This distribution clearly reflects the differences in the decomposition reaction pathways between AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI. Amorphous structures significantly influence the integrity of decomposition pathways by altering the local environment and diffusion behavior of reaction intermediates, thereby suppressing the formation of carbon-rich solid residues that are difficult to oxidize. Crystalline DATNBI (CEM-DATNBI) exhibits a dense, ordered molecular packing structure. During early pyrolysis, reactions may preferentially initiate at grain boundaries or defects. Partially oxidized intermediates (e.g., CO precursors) generated are restricted from diffusing out of the dense crystalline structure. These carbon-rich intermediates, “trapped” within or on the crystal surface, cannot fully contact oxygen for deep oxidation. Consequently, they are more prone to side reactions like polymerization and aromatization, ultimately forming highly thermally stable, non-volatile carbonaceous solid residues that resist further gasification. This explains the incomplete mass loss (77.3%) and relatively high CO yield. In contrast, amorphous DATNBI (AEM-DATNBI) exhibits a structure characterized by long-range disorder and large free volume. This structure provides more unobstructed pathways for the diffusion of reactants and intermediates. Consequently, intermediates generated during decomposition can rapidly diffuse and mix thoroughly with oxygen atoms originating from within the molecules, enabling a more complete oxidation reaction. This significantly suppresses the formation of carbon-rich solid residues, resulting in final reaction products consisting almost entirely of gaseous N₂O, CO₂, H₂O, and other components. Consequently, near-complete mass loss (97.4%) is achieved. In short, the difference in residue mass primarily stems from the amorphous structure inhibiting the formation of solid carbon residues, rather than simply altering the gas-phase ratio of CO and CO₂. The reduced CO yield results from more complete oxidation, not as a direct cause of decreased residues; the fundamental reason lies in the reaction pathway shifting toward more thorough oxidation, thereby avoiding the generation of solid carbon.

To quantify the energy landscape governing these processes, we employed Kissinger kinetics analysis on non-isothermal decomposition data (Figure 5c, Table 1, and Supplementary Fig. 25)55,56. It can be clearly seen that all fitted lines exhibit a good linear relationship (R2 > 0.96, Supplementary Table 3). The calculated activation energies demonstrate a 15.7% reduction for AEM-DATNBI (122.94 kJ·mol⁻¹) compared to CEM-DATNBI (145.91 kJ·mol⁻¹). This indicates that AEM-DATNBI requires less energy to activate molecules during decomposition, and amorphization helps reduce the energy barrier for thermal decomposition of the explosive, enhancing energy release characteristics. The findings align with the metastable energy state inherent to amorphous materials, providing fundamental understanding of structure-activity relationships in advanced energetic systems.

The impact tolerance increased by 150% (15 J vs. 6 J) and friction sensitivity (FS) reduced by 57% (252 N) compared to crystalline β-DATNBI counterparts (Fig. 5d). AEM-DATNBI exhibits a low mechanical sensitivity, which can be ascribled to its uniform internal structure and low-defect characteristics. These features reduce hot-spot nucleation in amorphous matrix. Further, using high-speed videography, we captured the flame combustion processes of CEM-DATNBI and AEM-DATNBI initiated by laser (Figure 5e). As shown in Figure 5e, AEM-DATNBI achieved a combustion rate of 56.5 mg/s, higher than that of CEM-DATNBI (45.2 mg/s), accompanied by intensified flame front propagation dynamics. This combustion superiority was further quantified through constant-volume chamber experiments measuring gas-generation kinetics (Figure 5f). The Pressure-time profiles revealed that AEM-DATNBI achieves faster initial pressurization rates (dP/dt) and 38% higher peak pressures than CEM-DATNBI (Figure 5g) demonstrating markedly enhanced reactivity. Notably, the observed single-stage gas release profile in amorphous systems contrasts with the multi-stage decomposition of crystalline materials, indicating optimized reaction continuity. This structural-kinetic relationship directly correlates with thermal decomposition activation energy reduction, confirming that amorphization establishes a continuous energy release pathway from thermolysis to combustion completion. Molecular-scale disorder eliminates lattice disruption energy barriers, accelerating combustion kinetics. It is evidenced the AEM-DATNBI achieving a 56.5 mg/s combustion rate, 25% faster than its crystalline counterpart (45.2 mg/s). and enhanced peak pressure in constant-volume tests. This metastable configuration concurrently lowers thermal decomposition activation energy (ΔE =122.94 kJ/mol), enabling rapid energy release.

Additionally, the detonation performance, as one of the core metrics for evaluating the application potential of explosives, was thoroughly explored in this study. Utilizing the EXPLO5 (version 6.02) software57, we systematically compared the detonation performance of AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI (Figure 5h). The results clearly indicated that the detonation velocity and pressure of AEM-DATNBI were significantly superior to those of γ-DATNBI, nevertheless lower than those of β-DATNBI and α-DATNBI. This discrepancy stems from the reduced density of DATNBI following amorphization, as detailed in the Supplementary Fig. 26. For energetic materials, the density metric is not the sole determinant of ultimate application performance. It is noted that amorphous materials can achieve favorable thermoplastic processing properties without reliance on polymeric binders. This characteristic implies that devices ultimately composed of pure energetic substances may surpass or equal the energy density of PBX (polymer-bonded explosives) systems containing inert binders58. Consequently, amorphous materials not only compensate for potential performance limitations arising from density differences but may even achieve superiority in certain aspects. Furthermore, the thermoplastic forming process enables the creation of uniform, dense charge structures. This microstructure shows promise for enhancing detonation performance, as it provides a more stable and efficient pathway for detonation wave propagation, which can contribute to faster and more complete energy release.

## Methods

Glass transition and melting temperature analysis
The thermal behavior of all samples was characterized using a NETZSCH DSC 204F1 Phoenix apparatus (NETZSCH-Gerätebau GmbH, Selb, Germany). Precisely weighed samples (~2 mg) in platinum crucibles, with an empty crucible as reference, were subjected to a controlled atmosphere under continuous nitrogen purge to prevent oxidative degradation. A two-step temperature program was employed (Supplementary Fig. 2a). In the first step, samples were heated from room temperature (T ) to T 10 K/min (Upscan 1), where T was maintained above the melting temperature (T ) but below the onset of thermal decomposition (T ). Subsequently, the melt was rapidly quenched to a sub-ambient temperature T₂ at 50 K min⁻¹ to facilitate glass formation. Following this, the quenched material was ramped back up from T₂ to a target temperature T proximal to T at 10 K/min (Upscan 2), with the specific objective of detecting the glass transition temperature (T )via analysis of the characteristic step change in the heat flow profile.

Preparation of AEM-DAATNBI
1,1ʹ-Diamino-4,4ʹ,5,5ʹ-tetranitro-2,2ʹ-biimidazole (DATNBI) was obtained from the Institute of Chemical Materials, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Initially, crystalline DATNBI (10mg) was positioned on a Linkam LTS420 heating stage to its melting point of 236.2 °C. Subsequently, the sample was permitted to melt entirely into a liquid state. The molten sample was rapidly quenched and cooled in liquid nitrogen to yield AEM-DATNBI. The resulting AEM-DATNBI was carefully removed and stored for subsequent use. The sunthesized AEM-DATNBI is transparent bulk material featuring a smooth surface and a homogeneous structure (Figure 2a). Notably, no elaborate workup procedures or specialized experimental equipment were employed during the formation of this glassy material.

Characterization
The morphology of CEM-DATNBI and AEM-DATNBI were analyzed by field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM), Ultra-55, Carl Zeiss. Samples were observed by Scope.A1 polarizing optical microscope (ZEISS, Germany). Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) spectra were collected on Bruker D8, with Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 1.54180 Å). X-ray total scattering data were then collected, with an X-ray generator providing Ag Kα radiation of wavelength 0.55941 Å. Samples were loaded into borosilicate glass capillaries of 0.5 mm (inner) diameter. Data from the samples, empty instrument and empty capillary were collected and processed using the PDFgetX3. The functional groups information of the samples was obtained by an infrared spectrometer (FT-IR, Tensor-27, Bruker, Germany), with the range of 600–4000 cm -1. Ultra-performance liquid chromatography−mass spectrometry (UPLC−MS) measurements were conducted on Thermo Fisher Scientific. The simultaneous differential scanning calorimetry and thermogravimetric (TGA-DSC, 1100L, Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland) analysis the thermoanalytical behaviour of the samples under a nitrogen atmosphere at heating of 5 K/min, 10 K/min, 15 K/min, and 20 K/min. The SAXS data used in this experiment are obtained by Xeuss2.0 small-angle X-ray scattering instrument produced by Xenocs company. For the laser ignition test, 20 mg of samples were radiated using a 10 W, 1064 nm infrared laser (MFSC-10, Maxphotonics) and recorded using a high-speed camera (VLEO410L, Photron). the pressure sensor (PC290) was used collected the pressure evolution with time of samples in a constant-volume vessel (300 mL)59. Safety properties were quantified through standardized impact sensitivity (IS) and friction sensitivity (FS) tests following the Bundesanstalt für Materialforschung (BAM) protocol60. Atomic force microscope (AFM) images were collected on a Bruker (SPA300HV Seiko). The contact angle and surface energy calculation of CEM-DATNBI and AEM-DATNBI were studied via a Kruss Scientific DSA100S model.

Activation energy (E ) calculation
a
The thermal decomposition behaviour of the samples was characterised by simultaneous thermogravimetric-differential scanning calorimetry (TGA-DSC, Mettler Toledo), where the sample mass of 2-3mg was placed in an alumina crucible, and the temperature programmer was set at a constant rate of 10 K/min from 30 ℃ to 500 °C under N atmosphere. Meanwhile the thermal decomposition behaviours of AEM-DATNBI and CEM-DATNBI were detected at different heating rates (5 K/min, 15 K/min, 20 K/min). The Kissinger method was utilized in this study to calculate the activation energy (E ) of thermal decomposition reaction55,56. there is a linear relationship between ln(β/T 2) and 1/T , and the kinetic parameters of thermal decomposition can be calculated by obtaining the T values at different heating rates and equations (1)
ln(β/T 2) = ln(AR/E ) - (E /R)(1/T ) (1)
where β is the heating rate (K/min), T is the thermal decomposition peak temperature (K), A is the pre-exponential factor, R is the ideal gas constant (8.314 J·mol-1·K-1), E is the activation energy (J mol-1).

Simulation and calculation details
To obtain the energetically favorable ground-state molecular geometries, quantum chemical calculations were performed using Gaussian 16W61. Density Functional Theory (DFT) with the APFD hybrid meta-GGA functional and the 6-31G(d) basis set; convergence criteria were maintained at the program defaults to ensure structural stability. The planarity characteristics of the optimized structures were subsequently evaluated through the calculation of two quantitative metrics using the Multiwfn program package (version 3.8)62. The Molecular Planarity Parameter (MPP), a scalar descriptor (ranging 0 to 1) quantifying global deviation from perfect planarity, and the Standard Deviation of Planarity (SDP), reflecting the root-mean-square deviation of atoms from the best-fit molecular plane and thus quantifying out-of-plane distortion. Finally, optimized geometries, computed molecular planes, and atomic deviations were rendered and visualized using the Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) software (version 1.9.3)63, enabling intuitive interpretation of planarity features and the spatial distribution of distortions.

The molecular dynamics simulation was carried out using Software Materials Studio. Firstly, 3×3×3 supercell for DATNBI (Supplementary Fig. 27) were constructed according to the unit cells. Then the supercells were optimized and energy-minimized using molecular mechanics (MM). The optimized supercells were relaxed using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations under NVT ensemble (with constant particle number, volume and temperature)64–66 at room temperature 298 K for 10 ps. Then the heating process was performed on each supercell with MD simulations under NPT ensemble (with constant particle number, pressure and temperature) 67 at 1000 K and 1 atm for 250 ps. The used temperature 1000 K is much higher than the melting points of the compounds, so that the melting process can be accelerated; meanwhile, during the simulations, the non-reactive COMPASS forcefield 68,69 was utilized to preclude chemical reactions at this high temperature. The melting cells were equilibrated under NVT ensemble at 1000 K for additional 50 ps. Finally, the supercells were cooled under NPT ensemble at 298 K and 1 atm for 250 ps, in order to obtain equilibrated glassy samples (Supplementary Fig. 28). Hydrogen bonds were characterized using conventional geometric thresholds, applying a donor-acceptor (D–A) distance limit of 3.0 Å and a donor-hydrogen-acceptor (D–H–A) angle threshold of 120°.

The density of the final amorphous supercells were measured, as well as the radial distribution function (RDF) was analyzed for each cell. The RDF gives a measure of the probability that, given the presence of an atom at the origin of an arbitrary reference frame, there will be an atom with its center located in a spherical shell of infinitesimal thickness at a distance, r, from the reference atom. This concept encompasses the principle that an atom at the origin and another at distance r may belong to distinct chemical species α and β, with the corresponding relationship formalized in equation (2)70.
ρg (r) = 1/N [∑Nα ∑Nβ δ(r-r +r)] (2)
where x is the mole fraction of chemical type i, N is the number of atoms of chemical type i, N is the total number of atoms, ρ is the overall number density, and g(r) is the RDF.

prior studies is crucial. To directly address the reviewer’s valid point and ensure that the unique

and Results & Discussion sections. Below, we respond to each of your comments in detail:
(1). We added a clearer context and brief descriptions of the methods in the introduction of the
revised manuscript. We have reframed the opening sentences of the abstract to explicitly state the
fundamental challenge of amorphizing rigid organic small molecules, such as energetic materials:
“Amorphous materials have penetrated various fields of modern technology. However, achieving
amorphous states in rigid organic small molecules remains fundamentally challenged by their
strong crystallization tendency, restricting deployment in defence and military domains like
explosives design".
Our introduction focuses on addressing the fundamental challenge of forming stable amorphous
states in rigid organic small molecules. Amorphous materials are critical across various fields due
to their unique disordered structure—characterized by short-range order but long-range disorder—
and their superior properties. However, rigid organic small molecules exhibit a strong inherent
tendency to crystallize and possess small steric hindrance, making the formation of stable
amorphous phases difficult and thereby limiting their practical utility. Current research
predominantly targets molecules with specific structural features (e.g., long alkyl chains,
polyaromatic rings, flexible linkers, or particular functional groups), leaving the amorphization of
structurally simpler rigid small molecules (such as mono- or bicyclic compounds) comparatively
underexplored.
Energetic molecules present an ideal model system to address this challenge of amorphizing rigid
small molecules, owing to their inherent high rigidity, high energy density, and tunable weak
intermolecular interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonding facilitated by nitro or amino groups). Crucially,
unlike pharmaceutical amorphization, which primarily aims to enhance bioavailability and
frequently relies on polymer additives or co-amorphous dispersant, energetic systems require
stabilization of the amorphous phase without compromising energy density. The strict avoidance
of exogenous components is therefore essential. This specific application context imposes more
stringent constraints on the preparation of amorphous organic small molecules.
To overcome this core challenge, our study employed structurally well-defined energetic
molecular systems. We implemented a functional group engineering strategy, modulating
molecular planarity, intermolecular interactions, and steric hindrance. This approach successfully
yielded a fully amorphous and homogeneous energetic material. We emphasize that this strategy
establishes a foundation for developing next-generation energetic materials characterized by stable
performance, rich functionality, and flexible processability. Furthermore, it provides a successful
paradigm for addressing the central challenge of low glass-forming ability inherent to rigid small
molecules.

special emphasis on elucidating its innovative aspects. To enhance the clarity and general
applicability of this core finding, we have expanded the systematic exposition of this mechanism.
Specifically, we have expanded the analysis of melt-processed energetic materials across three
primary categories: imidazole derivatives, benzene derivatives, and polycyclic compounds (Fig.

crystallization behavior, we explicitly elucidate the rationale of our molecular design strategy.

bonding network (via hydrogen bond donors/acceptors) is crucial for enhancing amorphous
stability, effectively strengthening intermolecular interactions and suppressing ordered
rearrangement. Building on this insight, the design strategy for DATNBI focuses on synergistic
effects. Initially, spatial hindrance is employed to reduce planarity (e.g., through backbone
modification and the introduction of flexibility), providing the foundation for amorphous
formation. Subsequently, the intermolecular hydrogen-bonding network is reinforced. DATNBI
was selected as a model molecule because it contains dual amino groups (strong hydrogen bond
donors) and dual nitro groups (strong hydrogen bond acceptors). This design aims to significantly
increase the density of hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, promoting the formation of a stronger
intermolecular hydrogen-bonding network. Furthermore, the inherent non-planarity of the
DATNBI structure, coupled with the synergistic effect of its bis-imidazole framework, increases
molecular conformational complexity and spatial hindrance (Fig. S15). This further reduces
molecular motional freedom, contributing to the maintenance of the disordered structure.

In summary, we establish a direct correlation between molecular structural features – specifically
the non-planar backbone and dual-NH₂/dual-NO₂ groups that reinforce hydrogen-bond networks –

rearrangement and hydrogen-bond networks strengthening intermolecular interactions). This

exceptional amorphous stability. In the revised manuscript, we have systematically reorganized
content regarding amorphous energetic material preparation and formation mechanisms to
emphasize this conceptual framework. We hope to provide a process framework suitable for
amorphization of rigid small molecules, which is applicable across disciplines in the fields of
photonics and semiconductors.

Building on this, the DATNBI design strategy integrates a synergistic dual approach: Firstly,
spatial hindrance (e.g., its bis-imidazole backbone and inherent non-planarity) is utilized to reduce
molecular planarity (MPP > 0.3), establishing the foundation for amorphous formation. Secondly,
the intermolecular H-bond network is significantly reinforced. The DATNBI molecule
incorporates strong H-bond donors (dual -NH₂ groups) and strong acceptors (dual -NO₂ groups),
markedly increasing H-bond density. The synergistic interplay between this non-planar molecular
scaffold and the dense H-bond network simultaneously increases molecular conformational
complexity and steric hindrance to restrict molecular motional freedom, while stabilizing the
disordered structure through intermolecular H-bond interactions. This synergy collectively enables
exceptional amorphous stability in DATNBI.

the non-planar backbone and the dual-NH₂/dual-NO₂ groups reinforcing H-bond networks—and
both the amorphous formation process (thermally induced lattice disordering/crystallization

and H-bond networks strengthening intermolecular interactions). This elucidates the multi-scale
synergistic mechanism underlying the exceptional amorphous stability of DATNBI. The core
synergistic principles identified are: (i) Molecular non-planarity (MPP > 0.3) suppresses
crystallization through steric disruption, and (ii) Intermolecular H-bond networks critically
enhance kinetic stability. This framework provides a strategy for the amorphization of rigid small
molecules, applicable across disciplines including energetic materials, optoelectronics, and
semiconductor devices, as detailed in the revised manuscript. all changes highlighted in red text
for ease of review.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this critical comment, which allows us to better
articulate the fundamental novelty of our work.
Although amorphous as a material state has been applied in multiple fields such as
pharmaceuticals, it is not an innovative concept in itself. However, its introduction into the field of
energetic materials represents a fundamental breakthrough. This integration is not a simple
technology transplant but rather a complete subversion of the long-standing paradigm in
explosives research, which has traditionally relied on crystalline structures. It has created an
entirely new material foundation of “amorphous energetic materials,” thereby opening an
unprecedented research direction. This breakthrough has pioneered an unprecedented research
direction, accelerating transformative advancements in explosive material development,
manufacturing processes, and performance enhancement, thereby opening new avenues for
exploration and innovation in the field of explosives. This manuscript successfully achieves the
stabilization and preparation of such high-energy rigid organic small molecules. With the unique
amorphous structure obtained, the material not only effectively suppresses hot spot formation and
significantly enhances safety but also simultaneously accelerates energy release, enabling faster
combustion and more complete decomposition. With a glass transition temperature of 59.67°C,
this material provides an ideal thermoplastic window for processing, laying the foundation for
future research on binderless forming of energetic materials. It not only simplifies manufacturing
processes but also avoids dilution by inert components, theoretically unlocking immense potential
for higher energy density in amorphous energetic materials. Thus, the emergence of amorphous
energetic materials pioneers an entirely new, unexplored research frontier in explosives science.
Its significance extends far beyond the discovery of a novel material, representing a paradigm shift
in research and a transformative future for the industry.
Regarding the references cited by the reviewers, we have conducted a detailed comparative
analysis. We contend that our work exhibits significant distinctions from these distinguished
studies. As noted in the references provided by the reviewers1, high molecular weight, structurally
complex and flexible organic molecules, their abundant functional groups and conformational
diversity, which facilitate the formation of amorphous states. In contrast, we concentrate on rigid
organic small molecules (typically comprising single or minimal ring systems substituted with
functional groups such as –NO₂ or –NH₂). Such molecules are widely recognized in the literature
as systems that are extremely difficult to form and stabilize in an amorphous state due to strong
intermolecular interactions and restricted conformational flexibility4. Therefore, this study directly
addresses the challenge of preparing amorphous states from rigid organic small molecules and
tackles the scientific problem of synthesizing amorphous energetic materials. Methodologically,
the pharmaceutical field employs solid dispersion technology for amorphization5-6, aiming to
effectively enhance the solubility and biocompatibility of poorly soluble components. However,
its characteristic of low drug loading capacity limits its application in the field of energetic
materials. The reason lies in the fact that energetic materials must strictly limit the proportion of
polymeric excipients to ensure their destructive effectiveness. This requirement further increases
the difficulty of manufacturing amorphous energetic materials. Instead, we selected a highly
challenging molecular system, expanded the application of amorphous materials into new domains,
and revealed a series of novel performance characteristics.
In response to the valuable comments from the reviewers, we have carefully revised the abstract
and introduction sections of the manuscript. This revision further clarifies the core scientific
questions addressed in this study while more prominently highlighting the distinctions between
our work and existing research, as well as the unique innovative value of our contributions.

(4) The real application of this method/materials as energetic material is doubtful, (I too have
commented that in my review) because of the lower density exhibited by amorphous materials.
Response: We are most grateful for your profound and constructive comments. The point you
raised concerning the impact of lower density in amorphous materials upon their application
potential is indeed a crucial issue within our research work. We fully concur that density
constitutes one of the core parameters for energetic materials. However, we think that the overall
performance and applicability of energetic material are determined by a balance of multiple
properties, and our work demonstrates that amorphous DATNBI offers a uniquely favorable
balance that can be highly advantageous for specific applications. In practical applications,
conventional crystalline energetic materials (such as TATB and RDX) exhibit brittleness, making
it difficult to meet the mechanical and structural requirements of weapon components through
direct pressing alone. Consequently, polymer bonded explosives (PBX) were developed and
widely adopted for manufacturing weapon parts. This technology involves dispersing high-energy
explosive particles within a polymeric binder matrix, thereby retaining high energy content while
achieving excellent processability and mechanical integrity1-2. However, since the binder itself
either does not participate or only minimally contributes to energy release, it reduces the energetic
density of the system, thereby diminishing both detonation velocity and pressure3. Thus, under
identical conditions of high-energy component content, PBX typically demonstrates lower density,
detonation velocity, and pressure compared to its pure crystalline form (Table 1). In contrast, the
amorphous energetic materials prepared in this study exhibit exceptional thermoplastic
processability owing to their unique glass transition characteristics, enabling the formation of
charges composed entirely of pure energetic components without relying on any binders. This
implies that although the density of the amorphous material may be lower, its charge density
equals its material density. As demonstrated by experimental data and reference (Table 1), typical
PBX charge densities (~1.8 g/cm³) are comparable to the density of our amorphous DATNBI
material (~1.89 g/cm³), with detonation velocities and pressures reaching 8,840 m/s and 34 GPa,
respectively—values that are either at the same magnitude or even more advantageous for the
latter. Therefore, in the final charge configuration, amorphous materials comprising 100%
energetic components hold promise for surpassing traditional binder-containing PBX systems in
overall performance.

Friction sensitivity was evaluated using a BAM friction sensitivity tester following the procedure
described in the UN Transport of Dangerous Goods, Manual of Tests and Criteria.
Impact Sensitivity (IS): The test was performed using a BAM Fallhammer apparatus according to
the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria. A 40 mm³ sample was taken using a cylindrical measure (3.7

following the same standard. For our powdered sample, a quantity of approximately 10 mm³ was
taken using a cylindrical measure (2.3 mm diameter × 2.4 mm deep) and placed on the plate. The

We sincerely appreciate the editors and reviewers for their time and valuable comments on
our manuscript. We are delighted that the reviewers found our previous revisions have

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
We sincerely thank you for your thorough review of the revised manuscript and for your valuable
suggestions. These recommendations have further enhanced the scientific rigor and clarity of
expression in our paper. We have carefully revised the manuscript according to each of your
suggestions. The specific modifications are as follows:
(1) In response to Reviewer #3, comment #4; The logic presented is generally acceptable; however,
the explanation requires some revision. The percentage formation of CO and CO is used to explain
2

is readily available both from the molecule itself and from the environment (since a standard TGA
instrument is not sealed against oxygen ingress). Given that both CO and CO are gaseous products,
2
it is unclear why carbon would remain in one case but not in the other. This point requires further
clarification.
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful and constructive comments. You correctly point
out that the total amount of carbon is conserved and that oxygen is obtained from molecules and the
experimental environment. We agree that explaining the difference in residue mass solely by the
ratio change of gaseous products CO and CO₂ without elucidating the underlying physicochemical
mechanism leading to solid carbon residue is indeed insufficiently clear.
Your question touches upon a key finding in our research. Amorphous structures significantly
influence the integrity of decomposition pathways by altering the local environment and diffusion
behavior of reaction intermediates, thereby suppressing the formation of carbon-rich solid residues
that are difficult to oxidize. Crystalline DATNBI (CEM-DATNBI) exhibits a dense, ordered
molecular packing structure. During early pyrolysis, reactions may preferentially initiate at grain
boundaries or defects. Partially oxidized intermediates (e.g., CO precursors) generated are restricted
from diffusing out of the dense crystalline structure. These carbon-rich intermediates, “trapped”
within or on the crystal surface, cannot fully contact oxygen for deep oxidation. Consequently, they
are more prone to side reactions like polymerization and aromatization, ultimately forming highly
thermally stable, non-volatile carbonaceous solid residues that resist further gasification. This
explains the incomplete mass loss (77.3%) and relatively high CO yield. In contrast, amorphous
DATNBI (AEM-DATNBI) exhibits a structure characterized by long-range disorder and large free
volume. This structure provides more unobstructed pathways for the diffusion of reactants and
intermediates. Consequently, intermediates generated during decomposition can rapidly diffuse and
mix thoroughly with oxygen atoms originating from within the molecules, enabling a more complete
oxidation reaction. This significantly suppresses the formation of carbon-rich solid residues,
resulting in final reaction products consisting almost entirely of gaseous N₂O, CO₂, H₂O, and other
components. Consequently, near-complete mass loss (97.4%) is achieved.
In short, the difference in residue mass primarily stems from the amorphous structure inhibiting the
formation of solid carbon residues, rather than simply altering the gas-phase ratio of CO and CO₂.
The reduced CO yield results from more complete oxidation, not as a direct cause of decreased
residues; the fundamental reason lies in the reaction pathway shifting toward more thorough
oxidation, thereby avoiding the generation of solid carbon.
We believe that the above modifications and clarifications have fully addressed your concerns and
provide a more in-depth and logically consistent explanation of the relevant mechanisms. Thank
you once again for helping us enhance the quality of our paper.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.
